report:
**Conclusion:** The claim that influenza vaccination causes Alzheimer’s disease is **false**. Extensive peer-reviewed evidence demonstrates the opposite: receiving a flu vaccine is associated with a significantly *reduced* risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease and other forms of dementia.

### Origins of the Myth
The claim originated in the late 1990s from unsupported assertions made by Hugh Fudenberg, a former doctor whose medical license was revoked in 1995 [[H. Hugh Fudenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._Hugh_Fudenberg)]. His claim that annual flu shots increase Alzheimer's risk has been thoroughly debunked by medical experts and public health organizations.

### What the Research Shows
Epidemiological studies consistently show a protective effect:
* **Lowered Risk:** A large cohort study published in the *Journal of Alzheimer's Disease* found that adults 65 and older who received at least one flu vaccine had a **40% lower risk** of developing Alzheimer’s disease over four years compared to unvaccinated peers [[PMC Article](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9484126/)].
* **Multiple Vaccines:** Research from UTHealth Houston showed that influenza, pneumococcal, Tdap, and shingles vaccinations are all associated with a lower incidence of Alzheimer's disease [[UTHealth Houston](https://www.uth.edu/news/story/several-vaccines-associated-with-reduced-risk-of-alzheimers-disease-in-adults-65-and-older)].
* **Systematic Evidence:** Systematic reviews and meta-analyses confirm that influenza vaccination consistently correlates with reduced dementia risk [[Frontiers in Immunology](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2022.872542/full)].

Researchers theorize that vaccines reduce brain-damaging systemic inflammation triggered by viral infections and may train the immune system to clear toxic protein accumulations in the brain.
